I.explanation: "I" with a capital letter means "you" when you speak to more than one person. It is not the English "I"; that is "jeg". Use "du" for one person and "I" for a group. Do not mix it up with "i" in small letters, which means "in".

sentence.en: Where are you all going this weekend?

at invitere.explanation: "At invitere" means to invite someone. "Jeg inviterer dig til min fødselsdag" means "I invite you to my birthday". You invite someone to something with "invitere til". The invitation itself is "en invitation". It is a regular word with simple endings.

sentence.en: I invite you to my birthday.

en idé.explanation: "En idé" is an idea. Note the accent on the e. You often hear "Det er en god idé" (That is a good idea) and "Jeg har ingen idé" (I have no idea). It is a very common word when making plans with other people.

en indkøbskurv.explanation: "En indkøbskurv" is the shopping basket you carry in a shop. It is for small shops, when you do not need a big cart ("en indkøbsvogn"). It comes from "indkøb" (shopping) and "en kurv" (a basket). The plural is "indkøbskurve".

sentence.en: I am taking a shopping basket.

en indkøbspose.explanation: "En indkøbspose" is the bag you carry your groceries in. It is built from "indkøb" (shopping) and "pose" (bag). In Danish shops you usually pay a small amount for a bag, so many people bring their own. A plain "pose" also works in everyday talk.

sentence.en: I have forgotten my shopping bag.

en indkøbsvogn.explanation: "En indkøbsvogn" is a shopping cart, the one with wheels you push in the supermarket. In many Danish shops you need a coin to unlock it, and you get it back when you return the cart. It is from "indkøb" (shopping) and "en vogn" (a cart). "Indkøbsvognen" means the shopping cart.

sentence.da: Du skal bruge en mønt til **indkøbsvognen**.
sentence.en: You need a coin for the shopping cart.

et indkøbscenter.explanation: "Et indkøbscenter" is a shopping mall, a large building with many shops under one roof. It is built from "indkøb" (shopping) and "et center" (a center). "the" goes on the end: "indkøbscentret". The plural is "indkøbscentre", and it is often shortened in speech to just "et center".

sentence.en: We are meeting at the shopping mall.

i.explanation: "I" means in, and it is used for places ("i Danmark"), months ("i juni") and how long something lasts ("i to timer"). Danish often says "i" where English uses another word, like "i dag" for "today". Do not mix it up with "på", which is used for many other places such as islands.

forms.en: What are you doing this evening?

i aften.explanation: "I aften" means this evening, the evening of today that is still coming. It is a fixed phrase and does not change. For the evening that has already passed, use "i aftes". Danes say it a lot when making plans.

sentence.da: Vi skal spise middag sammen **i aften**.
sentence.en: We are having dinner together this evening.

forms.en: I was at home last night.

i aftes.explanation: "I aftes" means last night, the evening that has just passed, usually yesterday evening. Do not mix it up with "i aften", which is this evening, still to come. It is used with the past form of verbs. For the sleeping hours, "i nat" is more common.

sentence.en: I watched a movie last night.

i dag.explanation: "I dag" means today. In Danish it is written as two words, "i dag". Use it for the current day: "I dag regner det" (It is raining today). The opposite pair are "i går" (yesterday) and "i morgen" (tomorrow). For the evening of today, say "i aften".

forms.en: What are you doing this afternoon?

i eftermiddag.explanation: "I eftermiddag" means this afternoon, the afternoon of today. It is a fixed phrase that does not change. Use it for plans and things that are still to come. For things that happen every afternoon, use "om eftermiddagen".

forms.en: I was sick the day before yesterday.
It happened the day before yesterday.

i forgårs.explanation: "I forgårs" means the day before yesterday, two days ago. It sits one step back from "i går" (yesterday). It is about a past day, so the verb is in the past. Note the "å" in "forgårs", the same letter as in "i går".

sentence.en: We met the day before yesterday.

i går.explanation: "I går" means yesterday, and it is written as two words. It is used with past events: "I går regnede det" (It rained yesterday). For last night, you say "i går aftes", and for yesterday morning "i går morges". The opposite is "i morgen" (tomorrow).

sentence.en: We were at the cinema yesterday.

i morgen.explanation: "I morgen" means tomorrow, and it is written as two words. For tomorrow morning you say "i morgen tidlig", and for tomorrow evening "i morgen aften". Do not mix it up with "en morgen" (a morning) or "om morgenen" (in the mornings), which are about mornings in general.

forms.da: Jeg stod op tidligt i morges.
forms.en: I got up early this morning.

i morges.explanation: "I morges" means this morning, but only when the morning is already over. It is for something that happened earlier today. Do not use it for a morning that is still to come: that is "i morgen tidlig" (tomorrow morning). It goes with the past form of verbs.

i nat.explanation: "I nat" can mean either tonight or last night. The tense of the sentence tells you which: with a future meaning it is tonight, with a past meaning it is the night that just passed. It is a fixed phrase, so there is no "the" in it.

forms.da: Er der en butik i nærheden?

i nærheden.explanation: "I nærheden" means nearby, in the area around you. If you add "af" and a place, it means near that place: "i nærheden af banegården". You will use it a lot when asking about shops, toilets or hotels. The opposite idea is "langt væk" (far away).

i orden.explanation: Means "all right" or "in order" and is used to say that things are fine or acceptable. "Det er i orden" can be an answer to an apology, like "no problem". "Er alt i orden?" is a polite check that nothing is wrong. It is a bit more formal than "det er fint".

forms.en: See you the day after tomorrow.
I am leaving the day after tomorrow.

i overmorgen.explanation: "I overmorgen" means the day after tomorrow, two days from now. It sits one step ahead of "i morgen" (tomorrow). It is the mirror of "i forgårs" (the day before yesterday). It is about the future, so it goes with plans.

sentence.en: Our guests are coming the day after tomorrow.

i skole.explanation: "I skole" means in school, as a pupil taking part in the school day. Danish drops the "the" here, in the same way as English says "in school" and "at home". To say "to school" you can say "i skole" too: "Jeg skal i skole". For the building, say "i skolen".

sentence.en: The children are in school now.

i stykker.explanation: "I stykker" means broken, or in pieces. It is used with "er" (is): "Computeren er i stykker" means the computer is broken. It does not change its ending. It means something physical is broken, not that a person has a broken heart. Another word is "itu", which means in two, which is a bit more formal.

i udlandet.explanation: "I udlandet" means abroad, in another country. For going there, Danes say "til udlandet", and for coming from there "fra udlandet". "Udlandet" is "udland" with "the" added on the end, so you say "i udlandet". A person from abroad is "en udlænding".

forms.en: What are you doing this weekend?

i weekenden.explanation: "I weekenden" is used for this weekend, both the coming one and the one that just passed, depending on the tense. The word "the" is added to the end of "weekend", so it is "weekenden". It is also used for the weekend in general: "Jeg sover længe i weekenden".

sentence.en: I am visiting my family this weekend.

i år.explanation: "I år" means this year, the one you are in now. It is a fixed phrase and does not change. For last year, say "sidste år", and for next year, "næste år". Use it with any tense, depending on whether it is something done or still to come.

sentence.en: We are going on vacation this year.

igen.explanation: "Igen" means again, and it also means back: "Jeg kommer igen" can be "I'll come back" or "I'll come again". In a Danish sentence it usually sits late. Do not mix it up with "også", which means also.

igennem.explanation: "Igennem" means "through" and is used when you go from one side of something to the other, as in "gennem skoven" or "igennem skoven" (through the forest). "Gennem" is a shorter version that means the same thing. It is also used for "all the way", as in "Læs det igennem" (Read it through). Use it for tunnels, doors, towns and more.

ikke.explanation: "Ikke" means "not". In a simple sentence it comes right after the verb: "Jeg kan ikke" (I cannot), "Han er ikke her" (He is not here). In a question it can come at the end, as in "Kommer du ikke?". If you want to say "no" as an answer, use "nej", not "ikke".

ikke endnu.explanation: Means "not yet". It is a handy short answer to questions like "Are you ready?". In a longer sentence, "ikke" comes after the main word and "endnu" usually goes at the end: "Jeg har ikke spist endnu" (I haven't eaten yet). Do not mix it up with "ikke mere", which means "no more".

ikke mere.explanation: Has two main meanings: "no more" (when you have had enough) and "not anymore" (when something has stopped). "Ikke mere, tak" is a polite way to refuse more food or drink. In a longer sentence it often goes at the end: "Hun arbejder her ikke mere". Compare "ikke endnu" (not yet).

sentence.da: Tak for mad, men **ikke mere**, tak.
sentence.en: Thanks for the food, but no more, thank you.

ild.explanation: Ild is fire in the sense of flames and burning. It is an en-word, so "the fire" is "ilden". Danish splits this idea in a few ways: "ild" is the flame itself, "en brand" is a fire that burns a house or forest (an emergency), and "et bål" is a campfire or bonfire. When something burns, you can say "Der er ild i huset" or "Der er brand".

sentence.en: The children sit around the fire.

imellem.explanation: "Imellem" means "between" and shows that something is in the middle of two or more things, as in "Jeg sidder imellem Anna og Peter" (I sit between Anna and Peter). It is also used for "sometimes" in the phrase "en gang imellem" (once in a while). The shorter word "mellem" means the same and is very common.

sentence.en: I am sitting between Anna and Peter.

ind.explanation: "Ind" means "in" when something moves from outside to inside, as in "Kom ind!" (Come in!). It is about movement. When someone or something is already inside, Danes say "inde" instead. "Ind" often goes with "i" to mean "into", as in "ind i rummet" (into the room). Its opposite is "ud" (out).

sentence.en: Would you like to come in?

inden.explanation: "Inden" means before, in the sense of before something happens. It often introduces a short part of a sentence: "inden jeg går" (before I go). For plain "before" with a time or a thing, Danes usually say "før" instead. "Inden for" means within.

indenfor.explanation: "Indenfor" means inside, and it is also the friendly invitation "Kom indenfor!" (Come on in!). It is sometimes written as two words, "inden for". With a time it means within: "indenfor en uge" (within a week).

indien.explanation: "Indien" is India. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Indien" means "in India" and "til Indien" means "to India". A person is "en inder" and the language is "indisk". Be careful: it ends in "-ien", not "-ia". "Indisk mad" is Indian food.

indisk.explanation: "Indisk" means Indian, as in from India, and is often used about food. It is written with a small letter and stays the same before an et-word. Use it for things from India. Native Americans are a different word in Danish: "indianer".

sentence.en: We are ordering Indian food today.

indtil.explanation: "Indtil" means until, and it marks the point when something stops. It works with times ("indtil klokken fem") and with a whole sentence ("indtil du kommer"). "Indtil videre" is a common phrase for "for now" or "until further notice".

influenza.explanation: "Influenza" is the flu, a stronger illness than a cold, often with fever and body aches. It is an en-word and many people shorten it to "influenza" or "flue" in speech. Say "Jeg har influenza" (I have the flu), without "en".

sentence.da: Jeg har **influenza** og skal blive hjemme.
sentence.en: I have the flu and have to stay home.

ingen.explanation: "Ingen" means "no one" or "none", and also "no" before en-words and many things, as in "ingen penge" (no money). It already means "not", so you do not add "ikke" to it. For "nothing" use "ingenting", and for et-words "intet" is also used.

ingen problemer.explanation: "Ingen problemer" means "no problem" and is a relaxed answer to thanks or to a request. "Problemer" is the plural of "et problem". You can also say "det er ikke noget problem". It sounds casual and friendly, close to English.

sentence.en: Can you help me? — No problem.

forms.en: Thanks for the help. Don't mention it.

forms.da: Ingen årsag, det var så lidt.

ingen årsag.explanation: "Ingen årsag" literally means "no reason" and is a reply to thanks, like "don't mention it". It is a little more formal than "det var så lidt". Another reply is "selv tak". Use it when someone thanks you for a small favour.

sentence.en: Thanks a lot! — Don't mention it.

ingenting.explanation: "Ingenting" means "nothing". It is made from "ingen" and "ting" (thing). Like "ingen", it already says "not", so you do not add "ikke". Another word you will hear is "intet", which is a bit more formal. The opposite is "alt" (everything).

interessant.explanation: "Interessant" means interesting. It stays the same for en-words and et-words ("et interessant sted"), and only gets "-e" for more than one. The matching word for the thing itself is "interesse", and "at interessere sig for" means to be interested in something. "Jeg er interesseret i musik" means "I am interested in music". The opposite is "kedelig" (boring).

internet.explanation: "Internet" is an et-word, so "the internet" is "internettet". Danes say "på internettet" for on the internet, and "online" is also very common. Because it is something you have rather than count, it normally has no plural.

is.explanation: "Is" means both ice cream and ice, so the situation shows what is meant. It is an en-word, so "the ice cream" is "isen". If you want to order a scoop, you say "en kugle is" (a ball of ice cream), and "en isbar" is an ice cream bar.

sentence.en: The children want ice cream after dinner.

island.explanation: "Island" is Iceland. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Island" means "in Iceland" and "til Island" means "to Iceland". A person is "en islænding" and the language is "islandsk". Do not mix it up with "is", which means ice.

isslag.explanation: "Isslag" is a weather word for rain that freezes as it hits the ground, making roads and paths very slippery. It is built from "is" (ice) and "slag" (a blow, a hit), and since "slag" is an et-word, so is "isslag". Weather services issue warnings for it, so it is a useful word to recognise in winter.

sentence.da: Der er varsel om **isslag** i nat.
sentence.en: There is a warning of freezing rain tonight.

italien.explanation: "Italien" is Italy. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Italien" means "in Italy" and "til Italien" means "to Italy". A person is "en italiener" and the language is "italiensk". Pizza, pasta and coffee all come to mind.

italiensk.explanation: "Italiensk" means Italian, for things from Italy and for the language. There is no capital letter in Danish. It stays "italiensk" before an et-word and becomes "italienske" for more than one thing. "Italiensk mad" (Italian food) is very popular in Denmark.
